findings.claim: Nobody ever looked at the button that completes the order on variant B.
findings.evidence: “Confirm purchase” sits about 180 px below the fold on the review step. Of the 9 agents who reached that step, 0 fixated it; on variant A the equivalent button was fixated by 9 of 9, median 2.3 s in.

findings.claim: A $9.95 service fee appears only after payment details are entered, and 4 of 9 agents left within 5 s of fixating it.
findings.evidence: The fee row holds 610 ms on first fixation and 2.4 revisits — the highest revisit count in the run. The total changes from $129.00 to $147.95 between the payment and review steps.

findings.claim: The promo banner takes the first fixation in 9 of 10 sessions, a median 1.3 s before any form field.
findings.evidence: Dwell 3.1 s with 1.8 revisits, against 1.2 s on the primary action beneath it. No agent applied the code: the banner costs attention without being used.

findings.claim: The payment step’s button says “Place order” but only advances to review, and 3 of 11 agents stopped there believing they had bought the boots.
findings.evidence: All three show a confirmation-seeking fixation pattern on the next screen (summary, then support link) and no further action. Their outcome is a failure with no order placed, not an abandonment.

findings.claim: On variant A, 2 of 11 agents abandoned at the cart after re-reading the shipping line.
findings.evidence: Both were the price-sensitive scanner persona; $8.95 shipping on a $129.00 order drew 2 revisits before they left. Reported for symmetry: variant A is the cleaner variant, not a perfect one.

findings.claim: 2 of 24 sessions ended in an automation failure and are excluded from both scores.
findings.evidence: Playwright selector timeout on the card-number iframe (S-09 on variant A, S-23 on variant B) after one retry each. This is a weakness of the simulation, never evidence against a variant.
